chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Sector Rotation Into Practice

lessons.title: Rotation Mistakes: Chasing Last Year's Winner, Overtrading, and Tax Drag

body.text: Most money lost in sector rotation is not lost by picking the wrong phase. It is lost by buying what has already worked, trading too often, and handing a fifth of every gain to tax along the way.

children.text: This lesson is the counterweight to everything before it. Using NSE index data, it shows what the most common rotation mistakes actually cost, starting with the one almost every investor makes at least once: buying the sector that just topped the performance tables.
Mistake 1: Chasing Last Year's Winner

Here is a simple, mechanical test. At the end of every calendar year from 2016, identify the best performing sector index among twelve major Nifty sector indices, invest everything in it for the next year, then repeat. Compare that with simply holding the Nifty 50. Returns are price returns from NSE closing values, with 2026 measured to 15 September.

children.text: Look at the pattern in the table. In 2017, Nifty Realty rose 109.8%, so the strategy bought realty for 2018, and it fell 33%. Pharma rose 39.1% in 2024, so the strategy bought pharma for 2025, and it fell 2.9% while the Nifty 50 rose 10.5%. PSU banks rose 30.5% in 2025, so the strategy bought them for 2026, and they have fallen 4.4% so far. Last year's return tells you almost nothing about next year's, and sometimes it tells you the opposite.

body.text: Notice that the chase strategy beat the index in half the years and still ended up well behind. That is the asymmetry of concentrated bets: the winning years add a few percentage points, while a single year like 2018 in realty takes a third of your capital. Hit rate is not the same as outcome.

The contrarian version, buying last year's worst sector, did even worse. The lesson is not "do the opposite of the crowd". It is that last year's return, in either direction, is not a cycle signal. Use the scorecard, credit and capacity data, and relative strength from Chapters 2 and 4 instead.

children.text: Mistake 2: Overtrading

Every switch costs money. Brokerage, securities transaction tax, stamp duty, GST on brokerage, the bid-ask spread, and any exit load all come out of your return before the sector has a chance to perform.

body.title: The Cost of Four Switches a Year
body.prompt: You invest ₹2 lakh for 10 years in sectors returning 12% a year before costs. You make four switches a year, and each round trip costs about 0.5% of the amount switched, so roughly 2% a year in total. How much less would you have after 10 years compared with paying no trading costs? Give the answer in rupees, rounded to the nearest ₹1,000.
body.explanation: Without costs, ₹2 lakh grows to about ₹6,21,170. With a 2% annual drag, it grows to about ₹5,18,748, roughly ₹1,02,421 less, or about a sixth of the no-cost outcome. Your sector calls now have to be good enough to overcome that 2% every single year, before tax.

children.text: Exchange trades attract brokerage, securities transaction tax, stamp duty, exchange fees, and GST on brokerage.
Thinly traded sector ETFs add a bid-ask spread that can cost more than a year of expense ratio in a single round trip, as Lesson 5.1 showed.
Active funds may charge an exit load if you redeem within the specified period.
None of these appear on your statement as a line called "trading costs", which is exactly why they get ignored.
Mistake 3: Tax Drag

Trading costs are small next to tax. Every profitable switch inside 12 months is taxed at 20% as a short-term capital gain, so the government takes a fifth of the gain before it can compound further. Holding for the long term defers the tax entirely and then charges 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh annual threshold.

body.title: Measure the Tax Drag
body.prompt: Using the table above, how much less does the annual switcher end up with after 10 years than the investor who simply held, in rupees? Round to the nearest ₹1,000.
body.explanation: The switcher ends with about ₹3,10,585 and the holder with about ₹3,66,486, a gap of roughly ₹55,901, or about 15% of the holder's final value. Both earned exactly the same 15% gross return every year. The difference is entirely tax timing. This is why rotation has to clear a high bar: your sector calls must beat the index by enough to cover both trading costs and this drag.

body.text: Two practical consequences. First, prefer fewer, larger, longer-held tilts over frequent switching. Second, where you expect to rotate often, a business cycle fund can defer the tax, since the manager's rotation inside the scheme is not a taxable event for you, as Lesson 5.3 explained.

children.text: Mistake 4: Buying the Theme After the Flows

Fund flows are a map of what has already worked. Sectoral and thematic funds attracted ₹46,137 crore in 2023-24, the largest inflow of any category that year, after a period of strong performance. By April 2026, after weaker returns, the same category drew only ₹1,949 crore of net inflows. Investors bought heavily near the top of enthusiasm and lost interest after the fall, which is the opposite of what the cycle framework suggests.

body.title: What the Crowd Does vs What the Framework Says

Buys new fund offers launched in the hot theme
Sells after a painful drawdown, locking in the loss
Judges a sector by its recent return
Adds tilts without capping total exposure

columns.label: Framework behaviour
points: Buys when the scorecard and relative strength turn, often before the return shows up
Checks whether a theme is early or late in its cycle
Exits when the thesis breaks, not when the price falls
Judges a sector by earnings drivers, valuations, and phase

children.text: The Six Mistakes and Their Fixes

cells: Use phase and relative strength evidence, not trailing returns
Set a review schedule and rebalancing bands; count the round-trip cost
Tax is invisible until you file
Plan holding periods; prefer fewer switches; consider a fund that rotates internally
Launches and headlines cluster near peaks
Treat heavy new fund activity in a theme as a late signal
Nobody wants to define failure in advance
Write the thesis and its exit conditions before buying
Confusing a structural theme with a cycle trade
Ask whether the driver is multi-year structural or cyclical, as Lesson 4.3 sets out

body.title: Go deeper: why a 50% hit rate still lost

children.text: The chase strategy beat the Nifty 50 in 5 of 10 years, yet ended up well behind it. The arithmetic of compounding explains why.
A 33% loss requires a 49% gain just to get back to even. Large drawdowns destroy more compounding than similar-sized gains create.
Concentrated sector bets produce both tails: the chase strategy had years like 2017 with 48.5% and years like 2018 with minus 33%.
Because you hold one sector at a time, there is nothing to offset a bad year.
This is the same logic as position sizing in Lesson 5.2: the size of your worst outcome matters more than how often you are right.
It is also why a diversified core plus small satellites survives being wrong, while an all-in rotation strategy may not.
Practice

body.title: Name the Behaviour
body.textWithBlank: Buying a sector fund because it topped the return tables last year is called performance ___, and the data in this lesson shows it lagged simply holding the Nifty 50.
body.explanation: Performance chasing treats last year's return as a forecast. Tested on twelve Nifty sector indices from 2016 to September 2026, buying last year's best sector each year returned less than the Nifty 50, despite beating it in half the individual years.

body.title: Read the Result Correctly
body.question: The winner-chasing strategy beat the Nifty 50 in 5 of 10 years but ended with +150.9% against the index's +182.2%. What does this best illustrate?
options: The test must be wrong, because beating the index half the time should mean higher returns
The size of losing years matters more than how often you win, because large drawdowns damage compounding
Sector investing never works in India
The strategy would work with more sectors
body.explanation: Winning half the time is irrelevant if the losses are bigger than the wins. A single 33% fall, as in realty in 2018, needs a 49% gain to recover. Concentrated, one-sector-at-a-time strategies make both tails larger, which is why position sizing and diversification matter more than hit rate.

body.title: Before You Rotate
steps: State the thesis in one line, drawn from the scorecard, credit and capacity data, or relative strength, not from last year's return
Check whether heavy new fund launches or media coverage suggest you are late
Calculate the round-trip trading cost of the switch
Check the holding period: would selling now trigger short-term tax at 20%?
Confirm the position size fits your satellite budget and per-sector cap
Write down what would make you exit, and when you will next review

body.title: Talk Down a Chase
body.scenario: In January, a colleague shows you a list of last year's best performing sector funds. One returned 46%. He wants to move 40% of his portfolio into it, sell after "a year or two of similar returns", and pay for it by redeeming a diversified index fund he has held for three years at a large profit.
body.prompt: Using the evidence from this lesson, what would you point out, and what would a better version of his plan look like?
body.modelAnswer: Three problems. First, the entry logic: a 46% year is not evidence about next year. Tested on twelve Nifty sector indices, buying last year's winner each year returned less than the Nifty 50 over nearly a decade, with cases like realty falling 33% after rising 110%. Second, size: 40% of the portfolio in one sector is not a satellite, and if it falls 40% his whole plan is damaged, which is the sizing point from Lesson 5.2. Third, the funding decision: redeeming a long-held index fund at a large profit triggers long-term capital gains tax and permanently removes the diversified core that makes being wrong survivable. A better version keeps the core intact, funds any tilt from new monthly investments or a small trim, caps the position at perhaps 5% to 10%, requires a written thesis from the scorecard rather than the return table, and sets exit conditions in advance. If he wants rotation without doing the work, a business cycle fund as one satellite defers the tax on switching, though it carries manager risk instead.

body.text: This lesson is educational. The strategy tests use price returns from NSE index closing values and exclude dividends, costs, and taxes unless stated; they are historical illustrations, not forecasts or advice. Tax rules and rates change; confirm your position with a qualified tax professional.

points: Buying last year's best Nifty sector index each year returned +150.9% from end 2016 to September 2026, against +182.2% for simply holding the Nifty 50
That strategy beat the index in 5 of 10 years and still lost, because single bad years such as realty falling 33% in 2018 destroyed the compounding
Buying last year's worst sector was worse again, at +86.2%: trailing returns are not a cycle signal in either direction
Four switches a year at 0.5% a round trip costs about 2% a year, roughly ₹1,02,421 on ₹2 lakh over 10 years at a 12% gross return
Tax timing matters even more: switching annually at 20% short-term tax left about ₹55,901 less than holding and paying 12.5% at the end, on the same 15% gross return
Fund flows follow performance: sectoral and thematic funds drew ₹46,137 crore in 2023-24 and only ₹1,949 crore in April 2026, after returns cooled
The fixes are structural: evidence-based entries, scheduled reviews, planned holding periods, capped position sizes, and written exit conditions
